paras: The attempted lynching of Major Hicks was an effort by an armed crowd from Ludlow, Kentucky, to take Hicks, a young Black man held in the Covington jail on a charge of murdering Henry Williams, on the night of December 17, 1880. Covington's marshal refused to give up the prisoner, and the crowd broke up after a few shots were fired, with no one reported hurt. Hicks was later convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to death, and three leaders of the mob were sentenced to jail terms and fines.

Williams, a young employee of the Cincinnati Southern railroad, was killed at Ludlow on a Wednesday night in December 1880. Later reports said he was killed for robbery, and the Indianapolis Leader described him as a white man. A Cincinnati dispatch of December 17 said Ludlow was "terribly excited" over evidence against Hicks, "a colored boy now under arrest," and predicted that he would "be instantly lynched" once the town was sure.

According to a Covington dispatch dated December 17, a crowd of 150 to 200 men gathered in a barn that night to lynch Hicks. Marshal Goodson placed Hicks in the most secure cell, armed his fifteen policemen with revolvers to command the jail entrance, and organized fifteen citizens with guns to patrol outside. Through the night a crowd of onlookers, "gathered by curiosity to see what might happen," stood about the jail.

At midnight a party from Ludlow, "armed in all conceivable ways," came to the jail and demanded Hicks's release, and the marshal refused. No organized attack followed, the dispatch said, though a few shots were fired. A later bulletin reported the crowd dispersing, and Hicks remained in the jail.

Hicks was indicted for the murder. In early March the Leader's Cincinnati correspondent wrote that circumstances favoring Hicks's innocence had led a prominent Kentucky lawyer to take his case, and urged Black Cincinnatians to attend a benefit concert at the Seventh Street Church for his defense. Two weeks later the column reported that the benefit, held at Union Chapel, had been poorly attended and raised little, and it described Hicks as poor, friendless and eighteen years old.

Hicks was tried in March 1881 before a special term of the Kenton County criminal court, and a Kentucky paper noted that he would talk with no one except in the jailer's presence. A Cincinnati dispatch of March 19 reported that the jury had found him guilty of murder in the first degree and fixed the penalty at death. He was sentenced to hang on June 10 and by mid-April had appealed.

In May 1881 three leaders of the December mob were sentenced to three months' imprisonment and fined $100 each. In January 1882, with Hicks still under sentence of death, a Lexington dispatch reported that Governor Blackburn had told his counsel that his illness with smallpox must not delay the execution.

White papers carried the mob story in December 1880 as a short Cincinnati wire, which treated a lynching as nearly certain, and as a fuller Covington dispatch that the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer headed "BOUND TO HANG HICKS" with the subhead that the mob was "Repulsed." Both treated Hicks's guilt as settled before any trial: the Rock Island Argus called him "the veritable assassin," and the Intelligencer's subhead called him "a Murderer."

When the verdict came in March, the wire explained the attempted lynching by the "cold-blooded" character of the murder and credited the "bravery of the officers" with preventing it. The New-York Tribune and the Washington Evening Star ran the same dispatch, and the Memphis Daily Appeal headed it 'A Colored "Majah" in Jeopardy,' with a dialect spelling of his title. Kentucky papers gave the trial and appeal one-line notes, and the May report on the mob leaders called Hicks "the negro murderer."

The Indianapolis Leader's Cincinnati column, written for the city's Black readers, took a different line: it doubted Hicks's guilt, warned that he might be "unjustly sentenced," and scolded Cincinnati people for leaving him without help.
The accounts differ on when the verdict came: the Cincinnati wire dated it March 19, the Evening Star said "last Friday," and the Interior Journal said he was tried on a Saturday.

framing.detail: December wire and dispatch: 'BOUND TO HANG HICKS', 'the veritable assassin', 'a Murderer'; mob 'Repulsed'.
March verdict wire treats the mob as a natural response to a 'cold-blooded' murder while praising officers' 'bravery' in stopping it; Memphis headline 'A Colored "Majah" in Jeopardy'.
Kentucky briefs note trial, sentence and appeal in one line each; May brief calls Hicks 'the negro murderer'.
Indianapolis Leader Cincinnati column (written for Black readers) recalls 'the attempt to lynch Hicks' and doubts his guilt, urging support for his defense.
